title: Identification of the Chicxulub crater
summary: In 1991, Alan Hildebrand, Glen Penfield, and colleagues published the identification of a massive, buried circular impact structure roughly 180 kilometers wide centered near Chicxulub Puerto on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. By linking Pemex geophysical surveys, impact melt rocks, shocked quartz, and Caribbean tsunami deposits, the team confirmed Chicxulub as the long-sought impact crater that caused the end-Cretaceous mass extinction 66 million years ago.

uncertainty.note: Seminal discovery paper published in Geology in September 1991.

as_recorded.value: Hildebrand A.R., Penfield G.T., Kring D.A., Pilkington M., Camargo Z.A., Jacobsen S.B., and Boynton W.V. (1991)

where.modern_name: Chicxulub Puerto, Yucatán, Mexico (coastal port situated above the buried center of the ~180-kilometer-wide impact crater)

importance.justification: Identifying Chicxulub provided the decisive physical crater linking the Alvarez iridium anomaly to the extinction of the dinosaurs.

related.because: The 1991 study identified the exact impact site of the 66-million-year-old Chicxulub bolide.
The 1980 Alvarez hypothesis motivated the decade-long global search for the Cretaceous-Tertiary impact crater.
